chapter_title: Building User Interfaces with Control Nodes
chapter_summary:
User Interfaces (UI) are the bridge between your game and the player. A well-designed UI is intuitive, responsive, and enhances the player experience, while a poorly designed one can be frustrating and detract from the game. Godot Engine provides a robust and flexible system for building UIs based entirely on `Control` nodes. Every UI element, from a simple button to a complex inventory screen, inherits from `Control`. Understanding `Control` nodes and their properties is fundamental to building effective UIs.

The `Control` node itself doesn't render anything visible by default, but it provides all the core properties for UI elements: position, size, anchors, margins, size flags, and input handling. The most crucial aspect of `Control` nodes for responsive UI is their **layout properties**:
*   **Anchors:** These define how a `Control` node's corners are attached to its parent's bounds. For example, setting all anchors to `(0.5, 0.5)` will center the node within its parent. Anchors are `Vector2` values from `(0.0, 0.0)` (top-left) to `(1.0, 1.0)` (bottom-right).
*   **Margins:** These define the distance from the `Control` node's edges to its anchors. If anchors are set to `(0,0)` and `(1,1)` (full parent size), margins define padding. If anchors are `(0.5, 0.5)` (centered), margins define the node's actual size relative to the center.
*   **Size Flags:** These tell parent container nodes how to resize their children. `Expand` makes a child take up available space. `Fill` makes it take up all available space in one direction. `Shrink Center` centers a child if there's extra space. `Shrink End` pushes it to the end. `Fill` and `Expand` are often used together in containers.

The true power of Godot's UI system comes from **Container nodes**. These specialized `Control` nodes automatically arrange and resize their children, making responsive UI much easier to manage.
*   **`HBoxContainer`:** Arranges children horizontally.
*   **`VBoxContainer`:** Arranges children vertically.
*   **`MarginContainer`:** Adds padding (margins) around its single child.
*   **`GridContainer`:** Arranges children in a grid, useful for inventories or complex forms.
*   **`PanelContainer`:** A `MarginContainer` that also draws a stylebox background.

Let's imagine building a main menu. You'd start with a root `Control` node (e.g., `MainMenu`) that fills the entire screen using anchors `(0,0)` to `(1,1)`. Inside this, you might use a `VBoxContainer` to stack your "New Game", "Options", and "Quit" buttons vertically. This `VBoxContainer` could be centered on the screen using its own anchors. Each `Button` inside the `VBoxContainer` would automatically be sized and positioned by the container.

Common UI elements you'll frequently use include:
*   **`Button`:** A clickable element. Its `pressed` signal is crucial for interaction.
*   **`Label`:** Displays static or dynamic text.
*   **`TextureRect`:** Displays a texture or sprite, often used for backgrounds, icons, or decorative elements.
*   **`ProgressBar`:** Visualizes a value within a range, like health or experience.
*   **`LineEdit`:** Allows users to input single-line text.
*   **`TextEdit`:** For multi-line text input.
*   **`CheckBox` / `CheckButton`:** For boolean options.
*   **`OptionButton`:** A dropdown menu for selecting from a list of options.

Interacting with UI elements primarily happens through **signals**. When a `Button` is pressed, it emits a `pressed` signal. You connect this signal to a function in your GDScript to perform an action, like changing scenes or opening an options panel.

```gdscript
# In a script attached to your MainMenu Control node

@onready var new_game_button = %NewGameButton # Using node path or @onready var new_game_button: Button = $VBoxContainer/NewGameButton

func _ready():
    # Connect the button's pressed signal to a function in this script
    new_game_button.pressed.connect(_on_new_game_button_pressed)
    # You can also connect signals directly in the editor!

func _on_new_game_button_pressed():
    print("New Game button pressed!")
    get_tree().change_scene_to_file("res://scenes/game_level.tscn")

# Example for a ProgressBar
@onready var health_bar = %HealthBar as ProgressBar

func update_health(current_health: int, max_health: int):
    health_bar.value = current_health
    health_bar.max_value = max_health
    # You can also update a label showing the exact health value
    # %HealthLabel.text = str(current_health) + "/" + str(max_health)
```

Common mistakes often involve not using container nodes, leading to manually positioned UI elements that break when the screen resolution changes. Always try to build your UI hierarchically with containers. Another mistake is forgetting to set anchors correctly, resulting in UI elements that don't scale or position as expected. When dealing with `TextureRect` nodes, remember to set `expand_mode` to `IgnoreSize` if you want it to respect the container's sizing, or `FitWidth/FitHeight` if you want it to scale while maintaining aspect ratio. For safety, always ensure your UI input is properly handled and validated, especially for `LineEdit` nodes, to prevent unexpected behavior or security vulnerabilities if you're dealing with network input. Also, be mindful of UI performance with complex `Control` hierarchies or many animated elements, as they can add overhead.

By leveraging Godot's `Control` nodes and container system, you can build robust, flexible, and visually appealing user interfaces that adapt gracefully to different screen sizes and provide a smooth, engaging experience for your players.

screens.title: Building User Interfaces with Control Nodes
screens.subtitle: Foundations, containers, common controls, and signal-driven interaction

narration.text: User interfaces are how players interact with your game. In Godot, every UI element inherits from the Control node. That makes the Control node the foundation you will use to position, size, and receive input for labels, buttons, bars, and input fields. In this lesson you will learn the essential layout properties — anchors, margins, and size flags — and how specialized container nodes take care of arranging elements so your UI remains responsive. You'll also see the common controls you will use every day: Button, Label, TextureRect, ProgressBar, and LineEdit, and learn how to wire their signals to GDScript functions so the UI can react to player input. The chapter includes a practical lab: building a responsive main menu with a centered vertical button stack and a bottom version label, and starter code that connects the buttons to simple functions. Throughout, I will point out common mistakes, like manually positioning controls instead of using containers and forgetting to set anchors, and show how to avoid them. By the end you will understand how to assemble a robust HUD or menu that scales across resolutions and reacts to player actions.

keyIdea.title: UI is Control-based
keyIdea.text: Every UI element inherits from Control; anchors, margins, and containers are the tools that make it responsive.

screens.title: The Control Node: What it is and what it provides
screens.subtitle: Control is the base class for all UI elements; understand its properties

narration.text: Define the Control node: it is the base class for all UI in Godot, not typically visible itself, but it provides the properties that make UI elements behave. Controls expose position and size information, anchors that attach corners to parent bounds, margins that set distance from those anchors, and size flags which instruct container parents how to distribute space. They also handle input events like mouse and keyboard interactions. A concrete example: a health bar Control child can receive input and be resized by its parent container without needing to compute pixel positions manually. A common misconception is thinking Control renders by default; in fact many Control types add drawing, but the generic Control only provides layout and input. That matters because layout logic belongs to Control, while visual appearance often comes from subtypes like TextureRect or custom drawing. Another misconception is treating anchors like margins — anchors set reference points in normalized parent space while margins measure offsets from anchors. Practical significance: get comfortable inspecting anchors as Vector2 pairs and adjusting margins to change size or padding. Try centering a panel by placing both anchors at 0.5, 0.5 and using margins to give it width and height. This clear separation of responsibilities—layout in Control, visuals in specific Controls—keeps UI predictable and easier to maintain. What small experiment will you try first to verify that Control is handling layout and not your script?

keyIdea.title: Control = layout + input
keyIdea.text: Control supplies anchors, margins, size flags and input handling; visuals come from specific Control subclasses.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Control Node
Control Node — Definition
The base layout and input node used by all UI elements.
Core properties
  • Position and size: derived from anchors and margins.
  • Anchors: normalized corners in parent space.
  • Margins: pixel offsets from anchors control size/padding.
  • Size flags: hints used by containers to resize children.
Common misconception
Control always draws UI. Actually, Control defines layout and input; visual rendering is provided by subclasses like TextureRect, Label or custom drawing.
Practical example — Centered Panel
Set both anchors to 0.5 and use margins to specify half-width and half-height around the center point. This centers and gives the panel a fixed size relative to the screen.
Check your understanding
  • What does anchors=(0.5,0.5) mean for the control's reference point?
  • How do margins change when anchors are full-screen versus centered?
Key Takeaway

Control organizes layout and input; learn to use anchors and margins before scripting positions.

screens.title: Anchors and Margins — how they determine layout
screens.subtitle: Anchors are normalized reference points; margins are pixel offsets from those anchors

narration.text: Anchors and margins are the two complementary pieces that define a Control's rectangle. Anchors are specified as Vector2 coordinates between 0.0 and 1.0 for each corner and attach the control's corners to positions inside the parent. For example, anchors at (0,0) and (1,1) make the control stretch to the parent's full size; anchors at (0.5,0.5) set both corners at the center, so margins determine the final size around that center point. Margins are pixel distances from each anchor: they behave like padding or explicit offsets depending on anchor setup. A concrete example: to create a centered dialog box, set left and right anchors to 0.5, use negative and positive margins to set width, and set top and bottom anchors likewise for height. A common mistake is moving the control in the editor without noticing that anchors were left at full-stretch, which causes unexpected resizing. Another mistake is assuming anchors are pixel values; they are normalized ratios of the parent's bounds, so they scale naturally with resolution. Why this matters: if you design a UI without consistent anchor and margin strategy, your layout will break when the window aspect ratio or size changes. Practice: place a control, toggle anchors between full, center, and corners, then observe how margins change meaning. That hands-on observation is the fastest way to internalize the relationship between anchors and margins.

keyIdea.title: Anchors vs Margins
keyIdea.text: Anchors set normalized reference points; margins set pixel offsets from those references — together they define size and position.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Anchors & Margins
Anchors and Margins — Process
Steps to reason about anchor and margin changes.
Step 1 — Choose anchor mode
Decide if the control should stretch with parent (anchors 0 to 1) or stay relative to a point (anchors at center).
Step 2 — Set margins
Use margins as pixel offsets from the chosen anchors to set padding or control size.
Example
Anchors left/right=0.5 and margins left=-150, right=150 produces a 300px width centered panel.
Quick checks
  • Does the control stretch unexpectedly after resizing? Check anchors.
  • Is the control the wrong pixel size? Inspect margins after adjusting anchors.
  • Are anchors set to normalized coordinates, not pixels?
Practical Tip

Use the Layout presets in the editor to quickly switch anchor presets and then fine-tune margins.

screens.title: Size Flags — how containers size their children
screens.subtitle: Expand, Fill, Shrink Center, and Shrink End explained

narration.text: Size flags tell a parent container how to allocate space among its children. The common flags are Expand and Fill; Expand requests the container to include the child when distributing available space, while Fill makes the child occupy all the space assigned in one direction. Shrink Center and Shrink End influence alignment when a child is smaller than the available space, centering or pushing it toward the end. Concretely, in a VBoxContainer you typically enable Horizontal Expand on buttons so they grow to fill the container width, and vertically you may not expand so the buttons keep a fixed height. A common misconception is using Expand on every axis regardless of context — this can create unexpected equal distribution and overflow. Instead, think which axis should stretch: for a horizontal list use Horizontal Expand, for stacked menus use Horizontal Expand on items and let the container control vertical stacking. Example: a set of three menu buttons with Horizontal Expand enabled will have matching widths, which simplifies visual alignment. When combining Fill and Expand, Fill controls how the child uses the space assigned, Expand controls whether it receives space at all. Practical significance: correct size flag usage reduces manual size calculations and ensures consistent spacing as the window resizes. Try toggling Expand and Fill on a child of a container to observe distribution changes and learn which flags produce the desired behavior.

keyIdea.title: Size flags influence container layout
keyIdea.text: Use Expand and Fill intentionally on the axis you want children to stretch; avoid enabling every flag by default.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Size Flags
Size Flags — What they do
Decide how a container distributes its available space to children.
Expand
Asks the parent to include this child when dividing extra space.
Fill
Makes the child fully occupy the space assigned in a direction.
Shrink Center / Shrink End
Alignment options used when children are smaller than the available space.
Example — Menu buttons
In a centered VBoxContainer, enable Horizontal Expand on each button so they match widths. This keeps visual balance as the window scales.
Pro Tip
Only expand on the axis you want to stretch. Overusing Expand can make children size equally when you don't want that.
Key Takeaway

Size flags let containers produce consistent layouts without manual pixel math; use them deliberately.

narration.text: Container nodes are specialized Control nodes that automatically arrange and resize their children, which is the core of building scalable UIs in Godot. HBoxContainer lays out children horizontally, VBoxContainer does so vertically, MarginContainer adds padding around a single child, and GridContainer arranges children in rows and columns—useful for inventories or option grids. PanelContainer is a MarginContainer that also provides a drawable stylebox background. A concrete example: an inventory screen is best built with GridContainer where each slot child has Expand flags so grid cells resize evenly. Misconceptions to avoid include trying to manually position items instead of leveraging a container; this typically breaks at other resolutions. Another subtle point: containers respect children size flags, so you must set Expand/Fill correctly on children to achieve the intended distribution. Practically, start every larger UI section with a container: menus inside a centered VBox, toolbars inside an HBox, and subpanels inside PanelContainers for consistent padding and background. That approach reduces code for layout and makes it easier to adapt as you add or remove elements. In the lab you will practice mixing containers: a root Control, centered VBox for menu buttons, and a bottom-anchored label. Thinking in containers first yields resilient, readable UI hierarchies.

keyIdea.title: Compose with containers
keyIdea.text: Build UI hierarchies from container nodes to avoid brittle absolute positioning and to gain automatic responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Containers Overview
Container Nodes — Quick Comparison
Choose the container that matches the layout pattern you need.
HBoxContainer
Arranges children horizontally. Use for toolbars and horizontal lists.
VBoxContainer
Stacks children vertically. Ideal for menus and stacked controls.
MarginContainer
Adds padding around a single child to create consistent spacing.
GridContainer
Creates a uniform grid; children sized by cell with Expand to distribute space.
PanelContainer
MarginContainer with a stylebox background; good for panels and dialogs.
Practical pattern
Compose containers: a root Control with nested VBox and HBox containers makes complex UIs manageable.

screens.title: Using VBoxContainer and HBoxContainer effectively
screens.subtitle: Stacking, separation, and expanding children for menus and toolbars

narration.text: VBoxContainer and HBoxContainer are among the most used containers for UI: VBox stacks vertically, HBox stacks horizontally. They manage child ordering and spacing via the Separation constant and respect each child's size flags when distributing available space. A practical menu: use a VBoxContainer centered in the root Control, add a Title label and several Button children, and set each Button's Horizontal Expand flag so they all share the same width. Adjust Separation to control vertical spacing between buttons. Common mistake: placing a Size Flag on the container instead of children; remember containers look at child flags to decide distribution. Another useful pattern is combining containers—a VBox where each row is an HBox allows complex, grid-like layouts without manual GridContainer configuration. Example: create a toolbar that is an HBox aligned to the top, with icon buttons that have equal width by setting Vertical Expand when necessary. Finally, when centering containers, prefer Layout presets in the editor and then fine-tune anchors and margins if the visual needs precise offsets. Understanding these small workflow details speeds up creating clean menus and toolbars that adapt to screen size without extra code.

keyIdea.title: Stack + adjust
keyIdea.text: Use Separation and size flags to make stacked or horizontal groups that scale and remain visually consistent.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › VBox & HBox
VBoxContainer — Menu Pattern
Center a VBox, use Separation for spacing, enable Horizontal Expand on button children for consistent widths.
Workflow
  1. Place VBox in root Control and set Layout to Center.
  2. Add Title label and Buttons as children.
  3. Set Separation and Size Flags on children.
HBoxContainer — Toolbars
Use for horizontal button rows; Vertical Expand on children ensures matching heights when needed.
Common mistake
Relying on manual offsets instead of Separation and size flags leads to inconsistent spacing when UI scales.
Key Takeaway

Use VBox for vertical menus and HBox for horizontal toolbars, and control spacing with Separation and size flags.

screens.title: GridContainer, MarginContainer, and PanelContainer
screens.subtitle: When to use grids, padding containers, and styled panels

narration.text: GridContainer is designed for uniform, grid-based layouts like inventories, option grids, or tiled selector screens. It places children into grid cells and is most effective when each child uses Expand flags so cells share available space evenly. A concrete scenario: building an inventory with a 4x4 grid of item slots—make each slot a child with Expand flags so the grid adapts to window size. MarginContainer wraps a single child with padding, useful for spacing a panel away from edges without adding extra nodes. PanelContainer combines MarginContainer behavior with a stylebox background, making it ideal for dialogs or framed panels. A frequent pitfall is using GridContainer for complex mixed-size layouts; if you need rows with varying column spans, consider nested containers or a custom control rather than forcing a GridContainer to do everything. Performance note: deep nested containers are fine, but many animations or thousands of controls can increase overhead; profile if you suspect UI bottlenecks. In practice, combine these containers: a PanelContainer to give a dialog background, MarginContainer inside for padding, and GridContainer or nested VBoxes/HBoxes for layout inside the dialog. This composition pattern keeps screens modular and easier to reason about as you iterate on UI design.

keyIdea.title: Use the right container
keyIdea.text: Grid for uniform cells, Margin for padding, Panel for styled backgrounds—compose them to build complex UI regions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Grid & Panel Containers
GridContainer — Inventories
Use Expand on slots and let the grid distribute space so cells resize consistently.
Practical example
A 4x4 inventory: each slot as a child Control with Expand horizontally and vertically will keep a uniform tile layout across resolutions.
MarginContainer & PanelContainer
MarginContainer adds padding to a single child; PanelContainer adds a background stylebox to create framed UI panels.
Best practice
Use PanelContainer to group a dialog visually and MarginContainer inside to create consistent internal padding.

screens.title: Common UI elements and configuration patterns
screens.subtitle: Buttons, Labels, TextureRect, ProgressBar, LineEdit and more

narration.text: Godot provides a set of Control subclasses for building interfaces. Button is the primary clickable control that emits the pressed signal; Label shows static or dynamic text; TextureRect displays textures such as backgrounds or icons; ProgressBar visualizes a numeric range like health or experience; LineEdit and TextEdit accept single-line and multi-line text input respectively; CheckBox or CheckButton provide toggles; OptionButton is the dropdown selector. For each element, learn the typical properties to tweak: for Button and Label you adjust font size and alignment; for TextureRect pay attention to expand_mode to choose IgnoreSize or FitWidth/FitHeight to control aspect ratio; for ProgressBar set value and max_value to reflect a measured quantity; and for LineEdit validate input since user text can originate from external sources. A concrete example: a health UI uses a ProgressBar with max_value set to max health and value updated from player state, while a Label displays exact numbers. Avoid the mistake of neglecting input validation on LineEdit when user input is transmitted or networked, and be mindful of style overrides for fonts to ensure legibility. The practical takeaway is to choose the right control for the job and configure its sizing and visuals with the same container + anchor strategy you used elsewhere.

keyIdea.title: Pick the right control
keyIdea.text: Use Button for clicks, ProgressBar for numeric visuals, TextureRect for images, and validate LineEdit input.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Common UI Elements
Common Controls & How to Configure Them
Button
Emits pressed; set font size and Expand for consistent sizing.
Label
Display static/dynamic text; set alignment and font overrides.
TextureRect
For backgrounds/icons; adjust expand_mode to control scaling behavior.
ProgressBar
Set value and max_value to visualize quantities like health.
LineEdit / TextEdit
Accept user input; always validate and sanitize external input when used in networks or saves.
CheckBox / OptionButton
Use for boolean options and dropdown selections in settings menus.
Key Takeaway

Match control types to tasks and configure their sizing and visuals with containers and anchors for reliable behavior.

screens.title: Signals and GDScript — connecting UI to game logic
screens.subtitle: How to connect pressed and update UI values in script

narration.text: Signals are Godot's event mechanism used to notify nodes of user interactions. Buttons emit the pressed signal when clicked. You can connect signals in the editor or programmatically. Programmatic connections make your code explicit and portable. In the attached example script for a MainMenu Control node you will see @onready variables that find child nodes and then connect the pressed signal to local functions. For UI updates like a health bar, the script sets the ProgressBar value and max_value from game state. A common mistake is forgetting to connect the signal or accidentally disconnecting it during scene changes. Another pitfall is referencing nodes before the scene is ready; use _ready to ensure nodes are available. The concrete code example in the content shows a simple MainMenu script — study how pressed connections trigger functions like changing scenes or quitting. When writing UI code, keep visual updates in response functions rather than polling every frame; this is both efficient and clearer. Finally, test signal handlers by clicking UI elements and watching print statements or visible state changes to be sure the connections are wired as you expect.

keyIdea.title: Signals connect UI to code
keyIdea.text: Connect pressed and other signals in _ready or in the editor; handle UI updates inside those handlers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Signals & GDScript
Connecting signals in code
Use @onready to reference nodes and connect signals in _ready for clear wiring.
extends Control

@onready var new_game_button = $VBoxContainer/NewGameButton
@onready var options_button = $VBoxContainer/OptionsButton
@onready var quit_button = $VBoxContainer/QuitButton
@onready var version_label = $VersionLabel

func _ready():
  new_game_button.pressed.connect(_on_new_game_button_pressed)
  options_button.pressed.connect(_on_options_button_pressed)
  quit_button.pressed.connect(_on_quit_button_pressed)

func _on_new_game_button_pressed():
  print("Starting a new game!")
  # get_tree().change_scene_to_file("res://scenes/game_level.tscn")

func _on_options_button_pressed():
  print("Opening options menu!")

func _on_quit_button_pressed():
  print("Quitting game!")
  get_tree().quit()
Common patterns
  • Connect signals in _ready to ensure nodes exist.
  • Keep UI updates inside handlers, not in process loops.
  • Use print statements during testing to verify handlers are called.
Misconception
Signals must only be connected in the editor. You can connect them programmatically for clearer and versionable logic.
Key Takeaway

Programmatic signal connections in _ready make UI behavior explicit and easier to test across scenes.

screens.title: Build a responsive main menu — step-by-step lab
screens.subtitle: Create MainMenu Control, center a VBoxContainer, add buttons and version label

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough shows the exact steps to build a responsive main menu. Start a new 2D scene and change the root to a Control node named MainMenu. Set the MainMenu layout to Full Rect so it fills the screen and becomes the reference for child anchors. Add a VBoxContainer as a child and set its Layout to Center to place it in the middle of the screen. Adjust the VBoxContainer's Separation to 15 to add space between children. Inside the VBoxContainer add a Title Label and three Buttons named NewGameButton, OptionsButton, and QuitButton. For the TitleLabel set horizontal alignment to Center and increase its font size; for each Button enable Horizontal Expand so they match widths. Then add a VersionLabel as a child of MainMenu but outside the VBoxContainer, set its Layout to Bottom Wide and adjust its offset to lift it slightly above the bottom. Attach the provided MainMenu script and, in _ready, connect each button's pressed signal to functions that print or quit. Run the scene, resize the window, and observe that the menu and version label maintain their positions and size relationships. As an extra challenge, add a TextureRect background and set expand_mode to IgnoreSize or FitWidth to learn how backgrounds interact with containers. This step-by-step practice cements anchors, containers, and signal wiring into a repeatable workflow you can reuse across menus and HUDs.

keyIdea.title: Lab workflow
keyIdea.text: Full Rect root, centered VBoxContainer, Expand on buttons, bottom-anchored version label, connect signals in _ready.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Main Menu Lab
Step-by-step
  1. Create a new 2D Scene and change the root to Control (rename MainMenu).
  2. Set MainMenu layout to Full Rect so it covers the viewport.
  3. Add a VBoxContainer child and set its Layout to Center; set Separation to 15.
  4. Add TitleLabel and three Buttons as children; set button font sizes and Horizontal Expand.
  5. Add VersionLabel outside the VBox, set Layout to Bottom Wide and offset it up slightly.
  6. Attach script to MainMenu and connect pressed signals in _ready to functions that print, change scenes, or quit.
  7. Run and resize the window to validate responsiveness; optionally add a TextureRect background and experiment with expand_mode.
Starter script
extends Control

@onready var new_game_button = $VBoxContainer/NewGameButton
@onready var options_button = $VBoxContainer/OptionsButton
@onready var quit_button = $VBoxContainer/QuitButton
@onready var version_label = $VersionLabel

func _ready():
  new_game_button.pressed.connect(_on_new_game_button_pressed)
  options_button.pressed.connect(_on_options_button_pressed)
  quit_button.pressed.connect(_on_quit_button_pressed)
  version_label.text = "Game Version: " + ProjectSettings.get_setting("application/config/version")

func _on_new_game_button_pressed():
  print("Starting a new game!")

func _on_options_button_pressed():
  print("Opening options menu!")

func _on_quit_button_pressed():
  print("Quitting game!")
  get_tree().quit()

screens.title: Troubleshooting and performance considerations
screens.subtitle: Common pitfalls with containers, anchors, textures, and input handling

narration.text: When building UI there are recurring pitfalls to watch for. First, avoid manually positioning controls without containers—manual placement often breaks when a window changes aspect ratio. Second, check anchors: controls anchored incorrectly can stretch or disappear unexpectedly. Third, when using TextureRect, set expand_mode intentionally: IgnoreSize lets the container govern sizing while FitWidth or FitHeight preserves aspect ratio but can leave empty space. Fourth, always validate LineEdit input if it's used in networked or saved contexts to prevent malformed data. Fifth, be mindful of performance: a very deep Control hierarchy or many animated UI elements can add overhead; profile and simplify the hierarchy if you see slowdowns. A concrete debugging approach: reproduce the issue by resizing the window, then inspect the suspected control's anchors and margins, and temporarily toggle container flags to isolate the cause. Use print statements in signal handlers to ensure the button pressed events are firing and that the correct functions are connected. Another common oversight is forgetting to connect or re-connect signals after instancing scenes dynamically; remember to connect signals in _ready for newly added nodes. Ending question for you: when your menu behaves oddly during resizing, which property will you inspect first and why? That habit of targeted inspection saves time during iteration.

keyIdea.title: Inspect, test, simplify
keyIdea.text: When UI breaks, inspect anchors and size flags first, test signal firing with prints, and simplify nested controls for performance.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting & Performance
Quick checklist to diagnose UI issues and avoid overhead.
Checklist
  • Inspect anchors and margins first when layout breaks.
  • Verify children size flags in containers to ensure correct distribution.
  • Test signal handlers with print statements to confirm firing.
  • Validate LineEdit input before using externally.
Performance tips
  • Simplify deeply nested controls when possible.
  • Avoid animating many UI nodes at once; batch updates in code where feasible.
  • Profile if the UI feels sluggish; controls do add cost when numerous or heavily animated.
Common mistake

Not using containers leads to fragile layouts. Start with containers to get reliable scaling; only resort to manual positioning for exceptions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Remember these core ideas as you build UIs. First, the Control node is the base for all UI and provides anchors, margins, size flags, and input handling. Second, anchors are normalized coordinates in the parent and margins are pixel offsets from those anchors; together they determine size and position. Third, containers like VBox, HBox, Grid, Margin, and Panel automatically arrange and resize children—use them to make responsive layouts. Each concept connects: controls provide properties, containers use those properties to lay out children, and signals connect UI elements to game logic. Practice building a centered VBox menu, connect button signals in _ready to GDScript, and resize the window to test responsiveness. Keep in mind common pitfalls like forgetting to set anchors or misusing size flags, and validate user input on LineEdit. These habits will make your UI robust, adaptive, and easier to maintain across different screen sizes.

keyIdea.text: Control + anchors + containers + signals = responsive, interactive UI.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for building robust UI

narration.text: Keep these three compact reminders close as you design UI. First, anchors are normalized and define how a control attaches to its parent—always think in relative terms. Second, use containers to express layout intent; they handle size distribution if children have the right size flags. Third, connect UI signals to script handlers in _ready and update visuals in those handlers; this keeps UI reactive without unnecessary polling. Practically, test your UI by resizing the window and by interacting with each control to ensure signals fire and layouts adapt. These quick checks catch most issues early and speed iteration.
